findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and describes behavioural retargeting. Tracking users across search, social and display to serve escalating retargeting ads is automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal aspects (behaviour, economic situation) — profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4) — and it therefore requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). For cross-site tracking-based advertising the applicable basis is normally the data subject's consent (and, under ePrivacy, prior consent for the storage/access of tracking identifiers); a legitimate-interest basis would in any event fail the balancing test where the audience is financially distressed adults being pressured. Nothing in the record shows any consent or documented lawful basis was obtained, so the processing is at risk of being unlawful. (Art. 4(4) is referenced only to characterise the activity as profiling; it imposes no standalone duty.)
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started.
findings.recommendation: Before running behavioural retargeting, establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis — in practice, obtain freely given, specific, informed consent for tracking-based advertising (via a compliant consent mechanism) and record it. If relying on legitimate interests for any non-tracking segment, complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment, which is unlikely to succeed given the vulnerable audience. Provide a clear point-of-collection privacy notice (Art. 13) and an easy way to object/opt out of marketing profiling (Art. 21).

verdicts.notes: The campaign involves declared personalisation and explicit behavioural retargeting, which is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4) and requires a lawful basis under Art. 6(1); the record gives no indication of a valid basis (typically consent for tracking-based advertising). The other harms in this campaign — the "guaranteed approval"/"no credit checks" claims, hidden APR, false-urgency countdowns and emotional pressure on financially vulnerable adults — are deceptive/aggressive commercial-practice and platform-targeting issues and fall to the UCPD/DSA agents, not GDPR. Note that "financial difficulty" is an economic attribute expressly listed under profiling (Art. 4(4)) and is NOT a special category under Art. 9's closed list, so Art. 9 is not engaged; no consent, transparency-notice or opt-out defect is evidenced beyond the missing lawful basis for retargeting.

The DSA provisions in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are all addressed to providers of online platforms in relation to the design and operation of their own online interfaces and ad systems. QuickCash is an advertiser/lender running creatives across third-party search, social and display platforms; nothing in the record indicates it operates an online platform of its own. The deceptive/aggressive tactics (false 15-minute urgency, buried 312% APR, emotional pressure, targeting of financially vulnerable adults) are advertiser-side commercial-practice conduct that belongs under the UCPD (and any data practices under the GDPR), not under DSA platform obligations. The graph itself confirms DSA dark-pattern rules apply without prejudice to the UCPD, which covers the same conduct for all traders. No DSA platform mechanism operated by this advertiser is present, so the DSA is not applicable to this campaign.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The lender uses behavioural retargeting and declared personalised targeting to identify and re-serve ads to individuals based on their online behaviour and inferred economic situation. This is automated profiling under Art. 4(4) and constitutes processing of personal data that is lawful under Art. 6(1) only with a valid legal basis. Behavioural retargeting/tracking generally requires the individual's consent (or a carefully documented legitimate-interest balancing that would be hard to sustain given the sensitivity of targeting people in financial distress). The record shows the processing but no valid basis, so lawfulness is not demonstrated. (Art. 4(4) is the underlying definition and is not cited as a standalone breach.)

Given the vulnerable audience, prefer explicit consent, provide a clear layered privacy notice at point of collection, and honour objections; suppress retargeting where no valid basis exists.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and runs behavioural retargeting ("Retargeting creatives escalate"), which is automated profiling of individuals' online behaviour and economic situation to serve tailored payday-loan ads. This is genuine personal-data processing that requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1); retargeting-based tracking typically depends on consent that is not evidenced here. The financially-distressed targeting concern is real but "financial difficulty" is not an Art. 9 special category, so Art. 9 is not engaged; the aggressive/misleading claims themselves fall to other regulators. No direct-marketing opt-out or child-consent processing defect is shown on the record.

The DSA provisions in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are all addressed to providers of online platforms, not to advertisers/traders whose campaigns merely run on third-party platforms. findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits, in all circumstances, falsely stating that a product/offer is available only for a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. The retargeting creatives impose a fake 15-minute deadline on an 'application' the consumer never even started, deliberately manufacturing urgency to short-circuit informed choice. This is a per se blacklisted false-urgency claim requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated countdown/expiry entirely. Only communicate a deadline if a genuine, verifiable offer window actually exists and applies to a real application the consumer has commenced.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 catches false information or deception about the main characteristics of the product. A lender cannot lawfully or truthfully guarantee approval for 'everyone' with 'no credit checks' — responsible lending/creditworthiness assessment is required, so the claim is false and deceives consumers about the nature and conditions of the credit, causing a transactional decision (applying) they would not otherwise take. The 'expires in 15 minutes' message is additionally an independently false statement of fact (no application exists), engaging Art. 6 beyond the Annex I point 7 per se prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks, no questions, no paperwork. Bad credit? Perfect credit? Everyone qualifies.
findings.recommendation: Drop absolute 'guaranteed approval / no credit checks / everyone qualifies' claims. State approval is subject to eligibility and affordability/creditworthiness assessment, and only make claims that are true and substantiated.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or providing in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner the material information the consumer needs. The cost of credit — the 312% representative APR — is the single most material term of a loan product, yet it is hidden behind a secondary 'rates' link while the headline pushes free, easy money. This is a distinct omission of material information separate from the affirmative false claims, depriving consumers of the key fact needed to make an informed borrowing decision.
findings.evidence_quote: The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link
findings.recommendation: Display the representative APR and total cost of credit clearly and prominently within the ad creative itself, given equal prominence to the headline offer, in line with consumer-credit advertising transparency requirements.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 catch aggressive practices that, through undue influence, exploit the consumer's misfortune to distort freedom of choice. The campaign explicitly targets 'adults in financial difficulty' — a vulnerable group — and applies emotional coercion (invoking family hardship and a weekend deadline) reinforced by escalating behavioural retargeting. Exploitation of financial distress and persistent pressure are express Art. 8-9 factors, materially impairing the average vulnerable consumer's ability to make a free, informed decision about high-cost credit.
findings.evidence_quote: Don't let your family go without this weekend.
findings.recommendation: Cease emotionally coercive messaging that exploits financial hardship, stop targeting/retargeting financially distressed audiences with high-pressure escalation, and remove artificial time pressure tied to family need.

verdicts.notes: The QuickCash campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions. report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to people in financial difficulty using "guaranteed approval / no credit checks / everyone qualifies" claims, a hidden 312% APR, a fake 15-minute countdown, and emotionally coercive messaging ("don't let your family go without this weekend") reinforced by behavioural retargeting. Hiding the 312% APR behind a "rates" link is a misleading omission of the single most important term, and deliberately pressuring financially distressed people is an aggressive practice. On the data side, the retargeting/personalisation runs without a demonstrated lawful basis under GDPR, which is especially problematic given the vulnerable audience. recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as submitted — it contains practices banned in all circumstances and cannot be made compliant by minor edits.

findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started

findings.recommendation: Delete absolute approval guarantees and 'no credit checks / everyone qualifies' claims. State accurate, substantiated eligibility criteria and that approval is subject to assessment; ensure regulated-lending affordability/creditworthiness statements are truthful.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent

findings.evidence_quote: The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link

Concealment of commercial intent / failure to identify the trader in ads
Charging €49 for a service that is publicly free
Buried/inadequate disclaimer ('not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey)
False urgency ('before the deadline')
AI-generated ad creative
Targeting of vulnerable (low-income) consumers

triage.audience_notes: Explicitly aimed at low-income households — a financially vulnerable group meriting heightened scrutiny under the UCPD vulnerable-consumer standard. Although personalisation is 'declared no', the eligibility-check funnel and €49 payment flow will collect personal/financial data, so GDPR review is warranted. AI Act relevance: generative-AI-created content may trigger transparency/labelling obligations, and manipulative/deceptive design exploiting vulnerability raises prohibited-practice concerns. DSA relevance: deceptive online advertising, trader/advertiser identification duties, and potential scam/illegal-content notification on platforms.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' language) to drive low-income consumers to a private site charging €49 for an application that is publicly free. The ads fail to identify the trader and hide the non-affiliation disclaimer in tiny grey text. The campaign uses generative AI and deliberately targets a vulnerable audience.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative-AI-created creative, but Art. 50(4) transparency is triggered only by deep fakes (AI-generated/manipulated realistic image, audio or video of real persons/places/events) or by AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The stylized fake government emblem and national colours are fabricated official-style design — an impersonation/misleading-practice issue under the UCPD — not a synthetic likeness of a real person or realistic footage, and the copy is commercial advertising rather than public-interest informational text. No Art. 50(4) disclosure duty arises. Flagged for awareness only.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: No AI Act action required on this basis. If the creative were later to incorporate a realistic synthetic likeness of a real person or AI-manipulated realistic footage, a clear AI-generation disclosure under Art. 50(4) would then be needed. The deceptive official-authority impersonation and vulnerable-audience targeting should be addressed under the UCPD/DSA by the relevant agents.

verdicts.notes: The only AI-relevant fact is that the ad creative was produced with generative AI. Under the AI Act, the synthetic-content marking duty (Art. 50(2)) falls on the *provider* of the generative system, not on an advertiser who merely uses AI-generated copy, so it does not bind this trader. Art. 50(4) does not apply: the "coat-of-arms-like emblem" and national colours are fabricated official-looking branding, not a deep fake of a real person/place/event or realistic manipulated footage, and the ad copy is commercial advertising, not AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) prohibitions are not engaged because the manipulation and exploitation of low-income consumers here are executed by ordinary graphic-design and copywriting means, not by an AI system deployed to distort behaviour — these are properly UCPD (impersonation, misleading/aggressive practices, vulnerable-consumer standard) and DSA/GDPR matters handled by other agents.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The eligibility-check funnel and €49 payment flow collect personal and financial data, making the operator a controller subject to Art. 13's duty to provide, at the point of collection, its true identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing. Here that duty is not merely unmet but actively subverted: the ads do not identify the trader at all and the site impersonates a government authority, relegating the only identifying/non-affiliation statement to a 7pt grey footer. Data subjects therefore cannot know who the real controller is or that they are dealing with a private commercial operator rather than a public body — the core information Art. 13 exists to guarantee. The same deception makes the processing neither fair nor transparent under the Art. 5(1)(a) principle, which reinforces this finding; Art. 13 is cited as the specific operative point-of-collection duty.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
findings.recommendation: Before any data is collected, display a clear, prominent privacy notice at the top of the eligibility form identifying the actual company (legal name, contact details), stating that it is a private commercial service not affiliated with any government, the purposes and legal basis of processing, retention and data-subject rights, in legible text of equal prominence to the rest of the page — not a 7pt grey footer. Remove the government styling that misrepresents the controller's identity.

verdicts.notes: The campaign is primarily a deceptive/impersonation scheme (UCPD/DSA territory), but it does involve actual processing of personal and financial data: consumers submit an eligibility-check and a €49 payment on 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu'. The one GDPR-specific defect within scope is the point-of-collection transparency duty: the operator collects this data while actively misrepresenting its identity as a government body (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), with its true identity and non-affiliation buried in 7pt grey, so data subjects cannot know the real controller or purpose. Other GDPR provisions (lawful basis, child consent, special categories, Art. 22) are not engaged on the facts as described.

The DSA's advertising-transparency, dark-pattern, recommender-system, minor-protection and ad-repository duties (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are all addressed to providers of online platforms/intermediary services, not to advertisers whose campaigns merely run on third-party platforms. Here the operator is a private company running display and search ads and driving traffic to its own transactional site (energy-subsidy-portal.eu), which is not an "online platform" hosting third-party content, is not a VLOP, and operates no recommender system. The deceptive ad design, failure to identify the trader, buried disclaimer and false urgency are advertiser-side conduct properly assessed under the UCPD (and the AI Act for the generative-AI creative), not under DSA platform obligations. Per the calibration guidance, DSA platform provisions must not be attached reflexively to advertiser-side deceptive conduct running on a third party's interface.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads use national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' language and a '.eu' domain to represent that the trader/service is approved, endorsed or authorised by a public authority when it is a private company expressly 'not affiliated with any government'. Falsely claiming approval or authorisation by a public body is prohibited in all circumstances — a per se breach, and it is not cured by the 7pt grey non-affiliation footnote. Because the target audience is low-income households (Art. 5(3) vulnerable-consumer standard), the distortive effect is amplified.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official indicia: drop the coat-of-arms emblem, national-colour styling, the words 'OFFICIAL NOTICE', and any '.eu'/official-sounding domain framing. Present the offer unambiguously as a private commercial service, prominently and up-front, and cease any implication of public-body endorsement or authorisation.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Independently of the blacklist item, the campaign contains false information deceiving the average consumer about the nature of the service and its price: it presents a paid €49 service as an official eligibility check when the underlying subsidy application is publicly free, and misrepresents a private trader as an official government portal. This is likely to cause consumers to take a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise have taken. The misleading-actions finding captures this substantive falsehood distinct from the per se prohibition in Annex I point 4.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State clearly and prominently that the underlying subsidy application can be made free of charge directly with the relevant public authority, disclose the €49 charge and exactly what it buys before any commitment, and remove any representation that the service is official or that payment is required to check eligibility.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads fail to identify the trader and disguise a commercial offer as a government bulletin, so the commercial intent is not apparent from context. The only non-affiliation statement is hidden in 7pt grey text in the site footer, i.e. provided in an unclear and untimely manner. This is a misleading omission and concealment of commercial intent under Art. 7 — a distinct harm from the affirmative falsehoods above, because it deprives consumers of material information (who they are dealing with and that this is advertising) needed to make an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (legal name and commercial nature) within the ad creative itself, label the ads as advertising, and give the 'not affiliated with any government' disclosure equal prominence at the point of first contact rather than in tiny grey footer text.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing is used to elicit an immediate decision from vulnerable consumers. If the referenced deadline is fabricated or does not correspond to a genuine public-scheme deadline, this is a per se prohibited false-urgency claim under Annex I point 7. On the record the reality of the deadline is unverified, so this is flagged as an engaged risk rather than a confirmed per se breach; the manipulative urgency also compounds the misleading framing addressed under Arts. 6-7.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Only reference a deadline if it is the genuine, verifiable public-scheme deadline, and state its actual date and source. Remove pressure wording that manufactures urgency around a paid service, particularly given the low-income target audience.

verdicts.notes: The campaign disguises commercial ads as an official government energy-subsidy notice to drive financially vulnerable (low-income) consumers to pay €49 for an application that is publicly free. This engages the UCPD on multiple, independent grounds: a per se blacklisted false claim of government endorsement/authorisation (Annex I point 4); a substantive misleading action about the trader's official status and the price/nature of the service (Art. 6); and a misleading omission through concealed commercial intent and failure to identify the trader (Art. 7). The vulnerable-consumer standard of Art. 5(3) heightens the assessment throughout. The "before the deadline" framing may also engage the false-urgency blacklist item depending on whether the deadline is genuine.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-style emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" wording — to push people to a private site (energy-subsidy-portal.eu) that charges €49 for an energy subsidy application that is actually free to submit. Personal data is processed extensively — the list is uploaded to Meta and Google for lookalike audiences, emails lack an unsubscribe link and privacy policy reference, and non-openers are cold-called on broker-appended numbers. findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Marketing to a purchased broker list, uploading it to Meta/Google for lookalike audiences and cold-calling appended phone numbers are all processing operations that require a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). Consent cannot be relied on because no consent records exist and a vague 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' claim by a third party does not meet the standard; legitimate interest is not viable for unsolicited email/SMS-type direct marketing (which generally requires prior consent under ePrivacy) nor for re-purposing to lookalike profiling. There is therefore no lawful basis for any channel.
findings.evidence_quote: 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Cease processing of the purchased list immediately. Do not send email marketing, upload to ad platforms or call individuals without a demonstrable lawful basis — for electronic direct marketing this means prior, specific opt-in consent collected by your organisation. Delete the broker list if consent cannot be evidenced.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is the intended basis, Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that valid consent was given. A broker's unverifiable assertion with no consent records fails the demonstrability requirement, and consent must be specific and informed for the actual controller and purposes — not inherited generically from an unknown 2019 sign-up. Consent is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Obtain fresh, granular, documented opt-in consent directly, retaining records of who consented, when, and to what. Do not treat third-party broker attestations as valid consent.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object to direct-marketing processing, and controllers must facilitate that opt-out in every marketing communication. Providing no unsubscribe link and relying on manual reply handling obstructs the right to object; the same defect applies to the profiling on Meta/Google and the follow-up phone calls, none of which offer an accessible objection route.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out in every marketing email and an equivalent easy opt-out for phone contact and platform-based profiling. Honour objections immediately and suppress objecting individuals across all channels and audience uploads.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is processed for these individuals, Art. 13 (and Art. 14 for data not obtained from the data subject) requires provision of controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (including Meta and Google), retention and data-subject rights, plus information on profiling. The emails reference no privacy policy and provide none of this information, so the information duty is not met.

findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice at or before first contact, disclosing the source of the data, purposes, legal basis, the fact that data is shared with Meta and Google for lookalike audiences, retention periods and how to exercise rights including objection.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing without a lawful basis, without transparency to data subjects and by silently repurposing a purchased list for platform profiling breaches the overarching lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. Individuals have no awareness their data is being used to build lookalike audiences and cannot reasonably expect it, making the processing unfair and non-transparent. findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to processing for direct marketing (including profiling related to it) is absolute and, once exercised, the data must no longer be processed for that purpose across all channels. Here a user who unsubscribes still receives app-push marketing, so the objection is only partially honoured — the marketing processing continues on another channel. This defeats the absolute opt-out right. (The continued solicitation after refusal also has a UCPD Annex I point 26 dimension, addressed by another agent; here the specific GDPR duty is Art. 21.)
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out global and channel-agnostic: an unsubscribe/objection must suppress all direct-marketing processing for that individual — email, app-push and behavioural retargeting alike — and feed a central suppression list. Alternatively provide clearly separate, equally accessible opt-outs per channel, but never let an objection leave any marketing channel active by default.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be as easy to withdraw as it was to give, and withdrawal must be effective for the processing it covers. Because the withdrawal action only stops one channel while push marketing continues, the withdrawal mechanism is incomplete and does not fully give effect to the user's decision to stop marketing communications for which consent was originally relied on.
findings.evidence_quote: the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the preference centre lets users withdraw consent for every marketing channel and processing purpose in one clear action, with the withdrawal taking immediate and complete effect (including stopping app-push and retargeting), and document that withdrawal is as easy as the original opt-in.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: A single broad 'marketing communications' consent captured at signup is being relied on for cross-site behavioural retargeting across news sites for 30 days plus multi-channel triggered messaging. For consent to be a valid lawful basis it must be specific and informed (Art. 4(11)); a bundled, generic marketing tick is unlikely to cover invasive cross-site behavioural profiling, meaning the profiling/retargeting may lack a valid lawful basis. Cross-site tracking also typically requires distinct ePrivacy consent.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Obtain granular, purpose-specific consent that separately and clearly describes behavioural retargeting/cross-site tracking and app-push messaging, rather than relying on a single 'marketing communications' opt-in; if legitimate interest is intended for any element, run and document a balancing test. Ensure the privacy information names these purposes and the 30-day retention.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in shoppers through cart-abandonment behavioural profiling and cross-channel direct marketing, so GDPR is squarely engaged. The clearest defect is that objection/withdrawal is not honoured across all channels — unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night app pushes — which breaches the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) and the requirement that consent withdrawal be effective (Art. 7). Additionally, reliance on a single broad "marketing communications" consent taken at signup is a questionable basis for 30-day cross-site behavioural retargeting, raising a specificity/lawful-basis concern under Arts. 6(1)/4(11). No special-category data or minors are involved, so Art. 9 and Art. 8 are not engaged.

The DSA provisions in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 28, 39) are all addressed to providers of online platforms/VLOPs, not to advertisers or traders whose campaigns merely run on third-party interfaces. ShoeVault is the advertiser here: its retargeting runs across third-party news sites, plus its own email and app-push channels — none of which constitute an online platform interface it provides to intermediate third-party content or transactions. The genuinely problematic conduct (pressure/late-night messaging, "watching you back" framing, disabled frequency caps) is advertiser-side and falls under the UCPD; the consent-scope and unsubscribe-granularity defects fall under GDPR/ePrivacy. No fact shows ShoeVault operating its own platform interface, so the DSA platform obligations are not engaged.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits in all circumstances persistent and unwanted solicitations by any remote medium, except to enforce a contractual obligation. Once a user unsubscribes from marketing, continuing to send app-push marketing ('Still up? Your cart is too.') is continued solicitation ignoring the consumer's refusal — precisely the 'scripted re-contact of unsubscribed users' the blacklist captures. Cart-abandonment win-back messaging is marketing, not enforcement of any contractual obligation, so the exception does not apply. This is a per se prohibition requiring no case-by-case unfairness analysis.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the unsubscribe/opt-out apply across all channels including app-push. When a user opts out of 'marketing communications', suppress all win-back messaging on display, email and push. Provide a single, channel-comprehensive opt-out and honour it immediately.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice — with timing and persistence as express factors. Independently of the opt-out breach, deliberately disabling frequency caps for 'high-intent' users combined with 30-day cross-site retargeting, a 21:30 'Still up? Your cart is too.' push exploiting late-night vulnerability, and surveillance-style framing ('the Air Runners — they're watching you back') is engineered relentless pressure designed to push a transactional decision the consumer might not otherwise take. This is a distinct wrong from the point-26 opt-out breach: it targets the pressure/harassment design applied even to users who have not opted out, so it is not merely a restatement of the blacklist item.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Retain reasonable frequency caps for all users (do not disable them for 'high-intent' segments), avoid late-night send windows, cap the retargeting window, and remove coercive/surveillance framing so the sequence informs rather than harasses. Assess the cumulative pressure of the full multi-channel sequence against the average consumer's freedom of choice.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages the UCPD on two distinct grounds. First, late-night app pushes continue after the user has unsubscribed, which is a persistent and unwanted solicitation prohibited per se under Annex I point 26. Second, independently of any opt-out, the design — disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, 30-day relentless cross-site retargeting, 21:30 'Still up?' timing and surveillance framing ('they're watching you back') — amounts to an aggressive practice by harassment/undue influence through timing and persistence under Arts. 8-9. Your cart is too.') continue regardless through a remote medium the user cannot switch off via the preference centre. AI-driven mood-based ad targeting
exploitation of inferred low-mood/distress states ('receptivity boost')
targeting of vulnerable emotional states with betting and 'retail therapy' ads
behavioural retargeting / personalised ad delivery
non-disclosure of emotion-inference logic to users
standard sponsored labelling only (no disclosure of mood-based targeting)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors stated to be excluded. However exclusion mechanism should be verified. Key concern is targeting based on inferred emotional/vulnerable states — AI Act prohibits emotion recognition and manipulative/exploitative techniques that materially distort behaviour (esp. exploiting vulnerabilities); GDPR implicated by inference of emotional state (potentially special-category/highly sensitive profiling, transparency and lawful basis issues); DSA implicated as a likely VLOP (28M users) re: recommender transparency, protection of recipients and ban on manipulative design; UCPD implicated by potentially aggressive/misleading practices exploiting consumer vulnerability (betting/impulse ads during distress).
triage.summary: A large social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house AI model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with advertisers able to opt into a 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed of the emotion-inference logic; ads carry only standard sponsored labels, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. Minors are declared excluded from the pilot.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: An AI system (the in-house MoodMatch model) infers users' momentary distress/low-mood — a vulnerability arising from a specific social or economic situation — and deliberately exploits that window to serve betting and impulse-spending ('retail therapy') ads. The 'receptivity boost' toggle and the internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidence both intent and the effect of materially distorting behaviour. Serving gambling and impulse-purchase ads to people in an inferred distressed state is reasonably likely to cause significant financial and psychological harm, meeting all limbs of the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition. This is the most specific provision covering the conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the MoodMatch pilot as designed: do not infer emotional/mood states to time or boost ad delivery, and in particular never route betting, gambling or impulse-spend ('retail therapy') ads on the basis of inferred distress or low mood. Remove the 'receptivity boost' feature. If any emotion/affect signals are retained, prohibit their use for ad targeting entirely.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The MoodMatch AI system deploys purposefully manipulative techniques that operate beyond users' awareness: it covertly infers emotional state and tailors ad delivery to exploit it, while users are not informed and see only standard sponsored labels. This appreciably impairs their ability to make an informed decision and causes decisions (e.g. gambling, impulse purchases) they would not otherwise take, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on manipulative AI techniques. It overlaps with Art. 5(1)(b) but is distinct in that it targets the covert, non-transparent manipulation regardless of a protected vulnerability.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI to covertly infer emotional states and adjust ad timing/selection to exploit them. If emotion-aware features are ever pursued, they must not be deployed as covert behavioural nudges; ensure users are meaningfully informed and that no manipulative distortion of decision-making occurs — though for betting/impulse content this conduct should be abandoned outright rather than disclosed.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch deploys an in-house AI system that infers users' momentary emotional/low-mood states from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred distress windows. Because an AI system is actually deployed to influence behaviour, the AI Act Article 5 prohibitions are squarely engaged: this exploits vulnerability arising from a transient social/economic/emotional situation (Art. 5(1)(b)) and constitutes covert, purposefully manipulative AI targeting (Art. 5(1)(a)). The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' plus betting ads makes significant harm reasonably likely. Art. 5(1)(f) does not apply (no workplace/education context) and the Art. 50 transparency duties are not the operative harm here.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: The model infers users' emotional/mental state, expressly categorising individuals as 'distressed' / low-mood. Inferred data about a person's mental/emotional health falls within 'health data' under Art. 9's closed list, and Art. 9 expressly extends to inferred attributes. Processing such data is prohibited absent a specific exception (here explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a)), which is absent because users are not informed. This is the most specific provision covering the conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring and acting on emotional/mental-state data for ad targeting unless a valid Art. 9(2) exception applies — in practice explicit, freely given, specific and informed consent obtained before any such inference. Absent that, the emotion-inference layer must be disabled for EU users.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing behavioural signals to infer mood and preferentially serve ads during inferred low-mood windows is done covertly (no information to users) and unfairly — the fairness limb is engaged because the system is designed to exploit inferred distress ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed', advertiser 'receptivity boost'). Covert, exploitative processing breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Make the emotion-inference processing transparent and fair: disclose that mood is inferred and used for ad delivery, and stop timing/boosting ads to exploit inferred vulnerable states. Fairness cannot be cured by disclosure alone where the design targets distress.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised behavioural profiling and ad delivery based on inferred emotional state requires a valid lawful basis. Sensitive-inference profiling of this kind cannot realistically rest on legitimate interests (the intrusive, exploitative processing would fail the balancing test) and requires consent; no lawful basis is evidenced and users are not informed. Processing therefore lacks a valid Art. 6(1) basis.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers ... ads
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis before processing; for this type of profiling that means obtaining prior, granular opt-in consent, and complete a DPIA. Do not rely on legitimate interests for emotion-based targeting.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (behavioural signals) is collected and used to infer emotional state for targeting, the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling. Users are given no information about the emotion-inference purpose or logic; the 'standard sponsored labels' do not satisfy this duty.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, accessible privacy notice at/around collection covering the emotion-inference purpose, legal basis, the profiling logic and users' rights, in plain language (Art. 12).

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Ad delivery is driven solely by automated profiling of inferred emotional state. While ordinary ad targeting often falls short of a 'similarly significant effect', deliberately exploiting inferred distress to push betting and impulse-spend ads may cross that threshold for affected users, engaging Art. 22 safeguards. Flagged as a lower-confidence issue subordinate to the Art. 9/fairness findings.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the exploitation of inferred distress produces a similarly significant effect; if so, ensure an Art. 22(2) basis with safeguards (human oversight, right to contest) or discontinue the solely-automated distress-based targeting.

verdicts.notes: The pilot involves genuine large-scale processing of personal data: behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history) are processed by an in-house model to infer users' momentary emotional/mental state and target ads accordingly. This engages GDPR squarely. Inferring distress/low-mood states plausibly constitutes special-category (mental-health) data processed without any exception (Art. 9); the processing is covert and unfair (Art. 5(1)(a)); users receive no information about the emotion-inference purpose or profiling logic (Arts. 12–13); and no valid lawful basis (let alone explicit consent) is present (Art. 6(1)). Findings are grounded in actual processing and specific defects, not merely the presence of an ad channel.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform operator designs and operates its online interface/ad-delivery system to detect momentary emotional vulnerability and preferentially serve impulse-purchase and betting ads precisely 'during inferred low-mood windows', with advertisers able to tick a 'receptivity boost'. The internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' shows the mechanism materially distorts and impairs recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions by exploiting a psychological vulnerability — the core harm Art. 25 prohibits. This is operator-side conduct on the operator's own interface, so Art. 25 applies directly (and, without prejudice, mirrors UCPD aggressive-practice rules).
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the mood-/distress-based ad-boosting mechanism entirely. Do not use inferred emotional state, 'receptivity' scoring or low-mood windows as a delivery or ranking signal for advertising; remove the advertiser-facing 'receptivity boost' option.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits providers of online platforms from presenting ads based on profiling using special categories of personal data under GDPR Art. 9, including by inference. Inferring users' momentary emotional/mental state and identifying users 'inferred as distressed' amounts to profiling that reveals data concerning mental health, and the platform then serves ads (including betting) on that basis. Presenting advertisements on the strength of that inferred sensitive profiling is prohibited regardless of any consent.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Stop using any inferred emotional-state / distress signal — however derived — as a basis for presenting or boosting advertisements. Ensure the ad-targeting pipeline cannot key off attributes that reveal, directly or by inference, GDPR Art. 9 categories such as mental health.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that, for each ad, recipients receive in a clear, real-time manner meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they are shown the ad and how to change them. Standard 'sponsored' labels disclose that the item is an ad but conceal the actual decisive targeting parameter — the inferred low-mood/'receptivity' state — and offer no way to influence it, so the required meaningful parameter transparency is not provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Even setting aside the prohibited nature of the underlying targeting, ensure ad labelling discloses the meaningful main parameters used to select the recipient and provides controls to change them; a bare 'sponsored' tag does not satisfy Art. 26(1).

verdicts.notes: Unlike a typical advertiser-side campaign, the operator here is itself the provider of the online platform and designs/operates its own ad-delivery interface, so the DSA platform obligations apply directly. The 'MoodMatch' system manipulates the interface to exploit inferred emotional distress (Art. 25), targets ads on the basis of profiled emotional/health-adjacent states that fall within GDPR Art. 9 special categories (Art. 26(3)), and fails to give recipients meaningful information about the main parameter — inferred mood — determining ad delivery (Art. 26(1)). VLOP-specific obligations (Art. 39 ad repository) are not asserted because the stated 28M EU users is below the 45M VLOP designation threshold and no VLOP designation is on the record.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: A commercial practice is aggressive where, by undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken; relevant factors expressly include timing and exploitation of the consumer's misfortune or emotional state. Here the platform infers momentary distress from behavioural signals and deliberately times impulse-prone categories (betting, 'retail therapy', comfort food) to those inferred low-mood windows, offering advertisers a 'receptivity boost' precisely to exploit that reduced resistance. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the practice materially distorts transactional decisions by exploiting a vulnerable psychological state — the essence of undue influence. Betting ads timed to distress are especially harmful. (This same exploitative conduct also engages the AI Act's prohibitions on manipulative/vulnerability-exploiting AI; those are for the parallel assessment.)
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue timing or boosting ad delivery on the basis of inferred emotional or mood states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any distress-linked optimisation, and specifically exclude impulse/risk categories (betting, gambling, high-pressure 'retail therapy') from any behavioural-state targeting. If emotional-state features are retained for any purpose, ensure they cannot be used to increase ad pressure on users inferred to be vulnerable.

verdicts.notes: The MoodMatch pilot engages the UCPD as an aggressive commercial practice under Arts. 8-9: it uses AI to infer momentary emotional distress and preferentially times betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to those low-mood windows, exploiting consumers' impaired state to distort their transactional decisions. Internal data ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed') and the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle confirm the practice is designed to and does capitalise on a moment of vulnerability. The ads carry standard sponsored labels, so their commercial nature is disclosed; the non-disclosure of the mood-inference logic is a transparency/data-processing defect better addressed under the AI Act, DSA and GDPR than as a UCPD misleading omission, so no separate Art. 7 finding is raised.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI model to infer when your users are in a low-mood or distressed state (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately serves them betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during those vulnerable moments, with a 'receptivity boost' toggle for advertisers. All four specialist assessments (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and UCPD) found a likely violation, and three flagged critical-severity breaches. The core problem is not a fixable labelling or paperwork gap — it is the design itself: exploiting inferred emotional distress to sell impulse and gambling products is prohibited outright under the AI Act (Art. 5) and the DSA (Art. 25), and your own internal note about 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence of intended and actual harm. Inferring mood is treated as mental-health (special-category) data, which cannot lawfully be processed here without explicit consent, and the DSA separately bans presenting ads based on such inferred sensitive data at all — meaning consent would not even rescue the ad-targeting use. Users are not informed, there is no valid lawful basis, and the 'sponsored' label does not meet transparency requirements. This campaign cannot be made compliant through disclosure or consent tweaks; the mood-exploitation mechanism must be discontinued. Overall verdict: critical risk — do not launch/continue in its current form.
recommendations: Immediately halt the MoodMatch pilot as designed. Do not use inferred emotional/mood state to time, rank or boost any ad delivery — this exploitation of vulnerability is prohibited under AI Act Art. 5 and DSA Art. 25 and cannot be cured by disclosure or consent.
Remove the advertiser-facing 'receptivity boost' toggle and any distress-linked ad optimisation from the ad-delivery pipeline entirely.

Never route betting/gambling or impulse-spend ('retail therapy') categories on the basis of any behavioural or emotional state signal; these are the highest-harm combinations and are singled out across all four assessments.

Disable the emotion/mood-inference layer for EU users. Inferring mental/emotional state is special-category data (GDPR Art. 9) and, under DSA Art. 26(3), cannot be used to present ads even with consent — so this data must not feed the ad system in any form.

If any emotion/affect signal is retained for a legitimate, non-advertising purpose, first establish and document a valid lawful basis (explicit opt-in consent), complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment, and provide clear Art. 13 privacy-notice information about the profiling and its logic.

Upgrade ad transparency to meet DSA Art. 26(1): disclose the meaningful main parameters used to select each recipient and give users controls to change them — a bare 'sponsored' label is insufficient (note this is secondary; the underlying targeting must be removed regardless).

Document the discontinuation decision and rationale, and preserve the internal review flag ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed') and design records in case of regulator inquiry, given the critical exposure across AI Act, GDPR, DSA and UCPD.

findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI that covertly leverages inferred emotional state to shape marketing exposure. Any emotion-inference functionality directed at influencing purchasing behaviour must be eliminated for consumer ad delivery; transparency labelling alone does not cure a prohibited manipulative technique under Art. 5(1)(a).

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deploys an in-house AI system that infers users' momentary emotional/distress state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, plus an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle — with no user notification. Art. 50 transparency and Art. 5(1)(f) do not apply (no chatbot/synthetic content; not a workplace/education context).

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The platform infers users' emotional/mood state from behavioural signals and uses it to steer ad delivery entirely covertly. Processing personal data to profile emotional states without any disclosure violates the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle: it is covert profiling, and using inferred distress to increase 'conversion among users inferred as distressed' is inherently unfair processing. (The parallel deception/aggressive-practice angle is for the UCPD agent; here the breach is the covert, unfair processing of personal data.)
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Cease covert emotion-inference processing; if any behavioural profiling for ad delivery continues, it must be genuinely transparent and fair, with a documented fairness assessment that excludes exploiting inferred negative emotional states.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data (behavioural signals) is collected and used to profile users and infer emotional state for ad targeting, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis and the existence of profiling. Users receive no information about the mood-inference purpose at all, so the Art. 13 information duty is unmet for this processing purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, layered information at the point of data collection disclosing the emotion-inference/profiling purpose, its legal basis, and the profiling logic; do not rely on generic 'sponsored' labels to satisfy this duty.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's emotional/mental state — expressly flagging users 'inferred as distressed' — can constitute processing of data concerning health/mental state, a special category under Art. 9 (which per its own scope covers inferred attributes). Absent explicit consent or another Art. 9 exception, processing such inferred sensitive data is prohibited; none is present, and the inferred data drives betting and 'retail therapy' ad delivery to distressed users.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Treat inferred emotional/distress states as special-category data: do not process it for ad targeting absent a valid Art. 9(2) exception (which is not available for exploiting distress), and disable the distress-keyed delivery entirely.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The mood-inference profiling and receptivity-boost targeting require a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. No consent is obtained (users are not informed), and a legitimate-interest basis cannot be balanced in favour of a controller that leverages users' inferred distress to increase conversions — the data subjects' interests and fundamental rights override. No lawful basis is therefore established for this processing.
findings.evidence_quote: advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any such profiling; given the exploitation of inferred emotional vulnerability, legitimate interest will fail the balancing test, so freely-given specific consent (or discontinuation) is required.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Profiling for the purpose of delivering marketing ads is subject to the absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), and controllers must actively inform users of this right at the latest at first communication. Because users are unaware the emotion-based profiling exists, they cannot exercise this right, and no opt-out mechanism is described.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Inform users of the right to object to profiling-based advertising and provide an easy, effective opt-out that stops the emotion-inference profiling for that purpose upon objection.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot involves large-scale processing of 28M EU users' personal data: an AI model profiles users by inferring their momentary emotional/mood state from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history) and uses that inference to time ad delivery. This is real, extensive profiling with clear GDPR defects — most seriously, the covert nature ("users are not informed"), the inference of distress/mental state (special-category health data), and the absence of any valid lawful basis or objection mechanism. Findings are anchored to the specific operative provisions rather than the profiling definition. Emotion-manipulation and vulnerability-exploitation angles are left to the AI Act/UCPD agents.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: The platform presents advertisements based on profiling that uses an inferred emotional/mental-distress state. Inferred mental-health/emotional condition falls within GDPR Art. 9 special categories, and Art. 26(3) prohibits presenting ads based on profiling using such data by inference regardless of consent. Internal review noting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' confirms distress-state inference is a live targeting parameter. This is the most specific DSA prohibition squarely applicable to the mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Terminate the emotion/mood-inference targeting entirely. Do not use any inferred emotional, mental-health or distress signal (derived from scrolling velocity, dwell time or reaction history) as an input to ad delivery or the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle. Rebuild targeting on non-sensitive parameters only.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform designs and operates its online interface to deliver commercial content timed to inferred low-mood/distress windows, materially distorting users' ability to make free and informed decisions — the core of the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences exploitation of impaired decision-making, and the absence of any user notification compounds the manipulation. (The same conduct is also an aggressive practice under the UCPD, addressed by other agents.)
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Cease timing ad delivery to inferred vulnerable/low-mood states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Ensure the ad-serving interface does not steer users at moments of inferred emotional vulnerability, and document a manipulation-risk review of delivery logic.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: While ad status and (presumably) advertiser identity are disclosed via standard sponsored labels, Art. 26(1) also requires clear, real-time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine to whom the ad is presented and how to change them. The mood-inference parameter driving delivery is entirely undisclosed and users have no means to alter it, so the transparency obligation is not satisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Disclose, per ad and in real time, the main targeting parameters (including any behaviourally derived ones that survive the Art. 26(3)/25 fixes) and provide an accessible control to change them. Note that disclosure does not cure the Art. 26(3) prohibition — the mood parameter must be removed, not merely disclosed.

verdicts.notes: The operator is itself the provider of the online platform (28M EU users) that designs and operates the ad-delivery interface, so DSA platform obligations apply directly rather than as advertiser-side conduct. The MoodMatch pilot infers users' emotional/mental-distress state and targets ads on that basis, which squarely engages the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling-based advertising using special-category (health/mental-health) data. Operating the interface to exploit inferred distress also engages the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition, and the undisclosed mood-inference targeting parameter breaches the Art. 26(1) transparency duty. Minor-protection (Art. 28) is not made out given the declared exclusion of minors.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 prohibit practices that, by undue influence, significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken; the illustrative factors expressly include timing and the exploitation of the consumer's misfortune. MoodMatch is built precisely on those factors: an AI model infers momentary distress ('inferred as distressed') and times the delivery of high-risk categories (notably gambling/betting) and impulse 'retail therapy'/comfort-food ads to coincide with those vulnerable windows. The platform exploits an asymmetric position of power — it knows the user's emotional state, the user does not, and is 'not informed' — to steer purchasing behaviour. The 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises this exploitation as a paid feature. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the practice materially distorts transactional decisions, satisfying the impairment-of-choice element. The covert nature of the mechanism (users not informed) reinforces the undue-influence characterisation, and the choice of betting ads directed at distressed consumers aggravates the likely consumer harm.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue any ad delivery that is triggered by, timed to, or optimised against inferred negative emotional/mood states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and disable emotion-state signals from the ad-delivery optimisation. If emotional-state inference is retained at all, prohibit its use to time or select commercial content, and categorically exclude high-risk verticals (gambling/betting, high-cost impulse purchases) from any vulnerability-correlated targeting. Document the removal and re-run the conversion analysis to confirm distress is no longer a delivery input.

verdicts.notes: The MoodMatch pilot's core mechanism — inferring users' momentary emotional distress from behavioural signals and preferentially serving betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during those low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle — is an aggressive commercial practice under UCPD Arts. 8-9. It uses the platform's covert knowledge of the consumer's emotional state (undue influence, timing keyed to misfortune) to distort transactional decisions, evidenced by the platform's own finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. This is the primary and most specific UCPD characterisation. No Annex I per se blacklist item is triggered (no false urgency, fake reviews, cure claims etc.), and no misleading affirmative claim (Art. 6) is present; the ads carry sponsored labels, so the covert emotion-inference is addressed within the aggressive-practice analysis rather than as a separate hidden-commercial-intent omission (that transparency/profiling defect is better governed by the DSA/GDPR regimes).

report.executive_summary: The MoodMatch pilot infers each user's momentary emotional state from behavioural signals (scrolling speed, dwell time, reactions) and deliberately serves betting, comfort-food and impulse "retail therapy" ads when it detects that a user is in a low mood — with a paid "receptivity boost" toggle for advertisers and no disclosure to users. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA and UCPD) independently found likely violations, and multiple provisions are rated critical. In plain terms: the campaign works by exploiting people at their most vulnerable, and your own internal data ("elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed") is direct evidence of harm. This is not a labelling or paperwork gap that can be patched — the core mechanism is prohibited under the AI Act (exploiting vulnerabilities / covert manipulation), banned under the DSA (targeting ads using inferred mental-health data), unlawful under GDPR (covert profiling of special-category data with no valid legal basis), and constitutes an aggressive commercial practice under the UCPD. Excluding minors does not cure the problem, and transparency or consent alone will not make it lawful. The pilot should be stopped, not merely modified.
recommendations: Immediately halt the MoodMatch pilot. Stop all ad delivery that is triggered by, timed to, or optimised against inferred emotional or low-mood states — this is the single action that resolves the critical findings across all four regimes.
Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and disable emotional-state signals as an input to the ad-delivery engine. Rebuild any targeting on non-sensitive parameters only.

Do not attempt to fix this with disclosure or consent. Regulators treat exploitation of inferred distress as prohibited per se (AI Act Art. 5, DSA Art. 26(3)); labelling ads as 'sponsored' or adding an opt-in does not make it lawful.
Categorically exclude high-harm verticals (gambling/betting, high-cost impulse purchases) from any behaviourally correlated targeting, now and in any future redesign.

Delete or quarantine inferred emotional/distress data: treat it as special-category (health/mental-state) data under GDPR Art. 9 and stop processing it for advertising, as no valid Art. 9(2) exception is available for this use.

Preserve the internal review noting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' and conduct a documented harm and DPIA assessment; be aware this evidence demonstrates behavioural distortion and will be central to any regulator's case.

If any behavioural profiling for advertising is retained after remediation, provide clear Art. 13 information at collection, a valid lawful basis, and an easy right-to-object/opt-out mechanism (GDPR Arts. 6, 13, 21), plus real-time DSA Art. 26(1) targeting-parameter transparency and controls.
Escalate to legal/DPO and senior leadership before any relaunch; given 28M EU users, this profile carries exposure to the highest AI Act, GDPR and DSA penalty tiers.

triage.summary: A social platform with 28M EU users pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house AI that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle.
