findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: An AI system infers users' momentary emotional state and deliberately times delivery of betting, comfort-food and impulse-spending ads to inferred low-mood/distressed windows. A distressed emotional state is a vulnerability arising from a 'specific social or economic situation'. Targeting it to drive purchases materially distorts behaviour, and the internal metric of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences both the exploitative objective/effect and likely significant harm — gambling and impulse spending pushed at emotionally vulnerable people are precisely the harms Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits. The 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises the exploitation for advertisers. This is a prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the MoodMatch pilot in its current form. Do not use inferred emotional/low-mood states to select, time or 'boost' ad delivery, and remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Emotional-state inference must not be used to trigger delivery of gambling, food or impulse-spending advertising to users identified as distressed.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Beyond the specific vulnerability exploitation, the system operates covertly: it infers emotional state and manipulates the timing of persuasive ad delivery beyond users' consciousness ('Users are not informed'). This is purposeful, AI-driven manipulative nudging that appreciably impairs users' ability to make an informed decision, causing transactional decisions (e.g. placing bets, impulse purchases) they would not otherwise have taken, with reasonably likely significant harm. This engages the manipulative-technique prohibition on a footing broader than any single protected vulnerability.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI that covertly infers emotional state to shape ad exposure. If any behavioural personalisation is retained, it must not exploit emotional inference and must be transparent to users; abandon emotion-derived targeting signals entirely for advertising selection/timing.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deploys an in-house AI system that infers users' momentary emotional/low-mood state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during those inferred vulnerability windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and no user disclosure. This is a live AI system used to influence behaviour, so the AI Act Art. 5 prohibitions apply directly. The exploitation of an inferred distressed state to drive conversions squarely engages Art. 5(1)(b) (and the covert manipulation dimension engages Art. 5(1)(a)). Art. 5(1)(f) (workplace/education emotion recognition) and the Art. 50 transparency duties are not applicable on these facts.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (behavioural signals) is processed to infer emotional state and drive ad delivery entirely covertly. Processing users' data to infer and exploit their momentary mood without informing them breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — this is hidden data processing and is materially unfair given it targets inferred distress. (Art. 4(4) profiling definition characterises the conduct.)
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Cease covert emotional profiling; if any behavioural profiling continues, provide clear, prominent information about the mood-inference logic and its use in ad delivery, and ensure the processing is genuinely fair (do not exploit inferred distress).

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Inferring emotional state and using it for behavioural ad targeting is processing that requires a valid legal basis. No consent is obtained and users are not informed; a legitimate-interest basis could not survive a balancing test where the purpose is to exploit inferred low-mood windows (internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed). No valid Art. 6 basis is present.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before any such processing. Given the intrusive, vulnerability-exploiting nature, only freely given, specific, informed consent could conceivably suffice; absent that, the processing must stop.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring that a user is in a distressed / low-mood state is an inference about the individual's mental and emotional condition, which can constitute health data within the closed Art. 9 list (data concerning health/mental state). Art. 9 covers inferred attributes. Processing such special-category data is prohibited absent an exception such as explicit consent, which is entirely absent here.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Treat inferred emotional/mental-state data as special-category data: do not process it for ad targeting without explicit, informed consent and an Art. 9 exception, and preferably discontinue distress-based targeting altogether.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The platform collects and further processes users' behavioural data to build emotional profiles and make automated ad-delivery decisions, yet provides no information about this purpose, the profiling logic or the existence of automated decision-making. Art. 13 requires purposes, legal basis, and meaningful information about automated decision-making/profiling to be disclosed at collection.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy notice/collection information to disclose the mood-inference purpose, the categories of behavioural data used, the lawful basis, and the existence and logic of the automated profiling and ad-targeting decisions.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Ad delivery is decided solely by automated profiling of inferred emotional state. Where this systematically targets users identified as distressed with betting and impulse-purchase ads, it can similarly significantly affect them (exploiting a vulnerable state to influence financial/gambling behaviour), engaging the Art. 22 restriction on solely automated decisions without safeguards, consent or the required transparency.
findings.evidence_quote: advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated distress-targeting produces significant effects; if so, do not rely on it without an Art. 22 legal ground and safeguards (human oversight, ability to contest, explicit consent), and exclude vulnerability-exploiting targeting entirely.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch processes real behavioural personal data (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history) of 28M EU users to infer momentary emotional/mood state and serve targeted ads — squarely a GDPR data-processing operation, not an incidental form/prize mechanic. The central defects are: covert processing with no user information (fairness/transparency), no demonstrated lawful basis, inference of mental/emotional distress engaging the special-categories regime, and solely-automated targeting that exploits inferred vulnerability. Findings cite the operative provisions; the profiling definition (Art. 4(4)) is referenced only to characterise the conduct, not as a standalone breach.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits a platform from presenting advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including — directly or by inference — health data. Inferred momentary emotional state / distress ('users inferred as distressed', 'low-mood windows') is inferred mental-health information within Art. 9, and the platform uses it as the determinant for which ads to deliver. This is prohibited regardless of any consent. This is the most specific prohibition covering the conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Terminate use of inferred emotional/mental-state signals as an ad-delivery or 'receptivity' parameter. Do not build or expose any targeting (including advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggles) that is derived from inferred distress or mood.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: As provider of the online interface, the platform designs and operates its ad-delivery interface to exploit users' inferred low-mood/distressed state — deliberately timing betting and impulse-spend ads to moments of impaired judgement, with internal review confirming 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. This materially distorts and impairs recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, contrary to the Art. 25 prohibition on manipulative interface operation. (The same manipulative/aggressive conduct is also reachable under the UCPD for all traders, but Art. 25 applies to the platform's own interface.)
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers ... betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers ... can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Remove the mood-timed delivery logic and the 'receptivity boost' mechanism. Ensure ad delivery is not organised to exploit inferred vulnerability, and document that the interface does not distort informed decision-making.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that the ad is shown to them and how to change them. A 'standard sponsored label' discloses that content is an ad but omits the actual main targeting parameter here — inferred mood/receptivity — and offers no means to change it. The transparency obligation is therefore engaged and not satisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Provide per-ad disclosure of the meaningful main parameters used to select the recipient and controls to change them. Given the Art. 26(3) prohibition, the mood parameter should be removed rather than merely disclosed.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: At 28M EU users the platform is likely a VLOP and must maintain a public ad repository including targeting parameters and reach (Art. 39). Ads run under this pilot, and their targeting logic, would be subject to public archiving and scrutiny. The record does not show a specific repository failure, so this is flagged for awareness rather than as a breach.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: If designated a VLOP, ensure the ad repository accurately reflects targeting parameters; note that documenting mood-based targeting there would publicly evidence the Art. 26(3)/25 breaches, reinforcing the need to remove the practice.

verdicts.notes: The operator is itself the online platform (28M EU users, a likely VLOP), so DSA platform obligations apply directly rather than under the advertiser-side carve-out. The 'MoodMatch' pilot squarely engages the DSA prohibition on ad targeting based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special-category data (Art. 26(3)), because it infers users' distressed/low-mood mental state and serves ads on that basis. It also constitutes prohibited manipulative interface operation (Art. 25) and fails advertising-parameter transparency (Art. 26(1)). Minors are excluded, so Art. 28 is not engaged.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise have taken; relevant factors expressly include timing and the exploitation of the consumer's misfortune. Here an AI infers momentary distress from behavioural signals and the platform deliberately times ads for betting, comfort-food and impulsive 'retail therapy' to those inferred low-mood windows — precisely exploiting a diminished emotional state to influence purchasing. The advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises this, and the internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the timing materially distorts transactional decisions consumers would not otherwise take. Exclusion of minors does not cure the exploitation of distressed adults. Art. 5's general prohibition and any misleading-actions angle are subsumed by this more specific characterisation.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot is a candidate aggressive commercial practice under UCPD Arts. 8-9: it uses AI to infer momentary distress and deliberately times betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to those low-mood windows, exploiting the consumer's emotional vulnerability through undue influence and timing. Internal data ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed') indicates a material distortion of transactional decisions. The ads carry standard sponsored labels, so ad-identification under Art. 7 is met; the non-disclosure of the emotion-inference/profiling itself is a transparency defect governed by the DSA/GDPR/AI Act rather than a UCPD misleading omission, so it is not reclassified here. The general unfairness clause (Art. 5) is subsumed by the more specific Arts. 8-9.

report.executive_summary: The MoodMatch pilot uses an in-house AI to infer users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and then deliberately serves betting, comfort-food and impulse-spending ads to people during their inferred low-mood windows — with advertisers able to tick a 'receptivity boost' and no disclosure to users. Every specialist that reviewed it found serious problems, and several are of the most severe kind. Under the EU AI Act this is very likely a prohibited practice: exploiting an emotional vulnerability (and covert manipulation) to distort behaviour, evidenced by your own 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Under GDPR, inferred emotional/mental state is treated as special-category health data being processed covertly with no lawful basis and no user information. Under the DSA, targeting ads on inferred mental-state data is flatly banned regardless of consent, and the mood-timed delivery is a prohibited dark pattern. Under consumer law (UCPD) it looks like an aggressive practice that exploits consumers' misfortune through timing. Excluding minors does not fix any of this — the harm to distressed adults is the core problem. This is not a fixable-with-disclosure campaign; the emotion-inference-for-ad-delivery mechanism itself must be stopped.
report.recommendations: Do not launch MoodMatch — halt the pilot immediately. The AI Act treats emotion-based exploitation of vulnerable users as a prohibited practice, and the DSA bans it outright regardless of consent, so no consent flow or disclosure will make it compliant.

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

animated brand overlays
streamer shout-out endorsements
discount code promotion
interest-based ad targeting (declared 18+ gaming interest)
high-caffeine product marketing without repeating on-pack warning in creatives
meme-format creatives appealing to young audiences

triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ but substantial known minor spillover (est. 34% aged 13-17), evidenced by analytics the brand receives — relevant to advertising to minors, high-caffeine product concerns, and DSA rules on minor-directed advertising and profiling. UCPD engaged for potential omission of material caffeine/warning info in overlays and influencer disclosure. GDPR engaged via interest-based targeting/personalisation and processing of audience analytics that may include minors.
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams with branded overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, using interest-based targeting nominally aimed at an 18+ gaming audience. Despite declared 18+ targeting and no requested profiling of minors, brand-received analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and creatives use meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The high-caffeine warning appears on pack but not in overlays.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Interest-based ad targeting is personalised advertising built on profiling (Art. 4(4)) of viewers' preferences and behaviour, which requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) — for behavioural/interest targeting typically consent or a properly documented legitimate-interest assessment. The record shows targeting is being carried out and that the brand actively receives audience analytics, but discloses no lawful basis, LIA or consent flow for this processing. The concern is heightened because the brand-received analytics reveal ~34% of the audience are 13-17, yet interest-based targeting continues without any evidenced basis or reassessment for that cohort.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the interest-based targeting and the analytics processing: either obtain valid consent for behavioural advertising or complete and retain a legitimate-interest assessment that accounts for the known minor spillover. Given the ~34% minor share, restrict or switch to contextual (non-profiling) placement where the audience cannot be reasonably confined to adults, and ensure the platform's targeting and analytics processing is covered by an appropriate legal basis in the controller-processor arrangements.

verdicts.notes: The campaign involves actual processing of personal data by the advertiser: interest-based ad targeting ("gaming interest, 18+") and receipt of audience analytics. This constitutes profiling/personalised advertising under GDPR (Art. 4(4) definition, cited only in rationale), which requires a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1). The record does not evidence a lawful basis, and the brand knowingly receives analytics showing ~34% of viewers are minors while continuing interest-based targeting. The minor-targeted-profiling ban (DSA Art. 28), UCPD disclosure/warning issues, and sensitive-data concerns fall outside GDPR or are not engaged here (no Art. 9 sensitive attributes, no automated significant decision, no data-collection form or consent-based children's service).

The DSA provisions in scope (Arts. 25, 26, 27, 28, 39) are addressed to providers of online platforms, not to advertisers whose campaigns run on a third party's interface. VoltRush is an energy-drink brand buying sponsorship/media on a third-party streaming platform; it does not operate the online interface, and targeting is performed "via the platform's declared-age targeting" — the platform's mechanism, not VoltRush's own. The Art. 28 minor-profiling ban binds the platform provider and, on the facts, is not even triggered advertiser-side ("no profiling of minors is requested"). The genuine concerns here (minor spillover, caffeine-warning omission in overlays, influencer disclosure) are advertiser-side conduct belonging under the UCPD, not DSA platform duties.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The high-caffeine warning is material safety information the average consumer (and, given ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, notably credulous/vulnerable members of the audience) needs to make an informed transactional decision. Presenting energetic, meme-format promotional creatives and a discount code while omitting the caffeine warning from the marketing communication itself withholds material information at the point of persuasion; that the warning appears only on pack (seen after purchase) makes its provision untimely for the purchase decision prompted by the stream.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, legible high-caffeine advisory (e.g. 'High caffeine content. Not recommended for children') within the animated overlays and any on-stream promotional creatives, displayed contemporaneously with the brand/discount-code prompt, not only on pack.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: The streamer shout-outs are paid/incentivised promotional content embedded in editorial-style live stream content. If the shout-outs are not clearly identified as sponsored, they constitute paid promotion presented as independent creator content, which Annex I point 11 prohibits in all circumstances; the same undisclosed material connection is also a misleading omission of commercial intent under Art. 7(2). The animated 'VoltRush' overlays are visibly branded, but a spoken shout-out woven into gameplay is not self-evidently an ad and requires explicit disclosure.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require the streamer to give a clear, prominent and durable sponsorship disclosure (e.g. spoken 'paid promotion by VoltRush' plus a persistent on-screen 'Ad/Sponsored' label) whenever the shout-out or discount code is delivered, and document this in the sponsorship contract.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires assessing practices likely to distort the behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (here, children/young teens) from that group's perspective. The brand's own analytics show it is aware ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, yet the creatives use meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens to market a high-caffeine product. This risks materially distorting the economic behaviour of a credulous, age-vulnerable audience contrary to professional diligence. No verbatim direct purchase exhortation to children is present, so the Annex I point 28 per se prohibition is not squarely triggered, but the fairness safety-net is engaged given the known spillover.
findings.evidence_quote: Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens.
